name: Dana Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, parties or government. This is confidential. What happens on your normal factory shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, and I feed dough into a biscuit divider on nights. I finished secondary school and came to this machine from packing less than a year ago, so the lead still checks my first tray after a size change. I like seeing each biscuit land in the same place; a sticky roller can turn a whole batch into crumbs.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are your pay, home and use of new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner Leon works daytime maintenance in a hospital, and our grown children live elsewhere. The night premium gives me higher pay than most operators, we have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other food plants nearby. I use AI occasionally to make sense of an oven notice, after a colleague checks it; I would not set the divider from a chat answer. Retirement is approaching as a decision, but we have not compared the actual income with our rent and living costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the night crew that AI can shorten the order sheet, but a biscuit still has to come off the divider at the right weight. I would keep the first tray on the bench until the lead says the size is right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The night rate and Leon's hospital pay cover our rent, and ten months saved gives us a buffer if a line stops. This small office change would not shorten my hours. I am still learning the divider, which is quite enough novelty for some shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep setting the divider with the lead and weighing the first tray after each size change. From each full paid month I would add a new amount to our savings after rent and groceries; the AI notice search I already use would stay occasional.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about work and money here. A tray of evenly sized biscuits is a better sign than a polished order report.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What went wrong on a recent first tray?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday one roller held dough and the first ten biscuits came out too light. The lead had me stop the feed and clean it before another tray. A biscuit order sheet cannot put missing dough back on a tray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why add savings if you have ten months already?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retirement income is not measured yet, and the night premium may not last forever. I would add only from new wages after costs, not give old savings a new label and call it growth.

say: I would tell colleagues **biscuit weight** still needs a first-tray check.
A faster **order sheet** cannot repair a sticky divider roller.
think: Our **night premium** and Leon's pay make current bills manageable.
Ten months of **savings** provide room while my machine work stays needed.
do: **Keep** feeding the biscuit divider and weighing first trays with the lead.
**Save** fresh full-month wages after rent and groceries.
feel: **Calm** about current shifts, while still learning the divider.
S0.quote: A biscuit order sheet cannot put missing dough back on a tray.
fieldNote: Her **junior machine skill** shows in first-tray checks with the lead, despite a high night-shift rate.
New **reserve additions** come from full paid months; her existing ten-month cushion is not counted twice.

steps.text: Keep running biscuit divider and weighing first trays with lead
Save new wages from full night-rate months after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI might plan flour orders and write rosters before robots can scrape a jammed roller. I would want the night hours posted before the office counts a faster sheet as a shorter shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The divider still needs hands, but software might spread the same work across fewer night shifts and take away the premium I rely on. Leon's pay and ten months saved help, yet a lower rate would change our monthly sums. I am open to a new camera after someone else proves it catches a light biscuit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed night roster with my last four wage slips and ask a day-shift operator what happened on a full camera trial. If the plant offers paid supervised time on a guarded test tray, I would learn the new AI weight-check display and verify each mark with the scale. If my paid night hours fall, I would apply only to posted nearby food-machine jobs whose safe duties, base wage after travel and shift times cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about losing the night premium, though I can check a real machine before deciding. A camera that catches the wrong tray is another job for me, not a saving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which test would convince you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put one light biscuit, one broken biscuit and one good one through a scrap run, then compare the camera marks with my scale. The lead should watch the first test on paid time with the guard in place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a day job nearby?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if its posted wage after bus fare still covers rent and food. A day shift might be easier to sleep around. A nice schedule cannot pay a shortfall.

say: I would ask for **posted night hours** before software changes the premium.
A new **weight camera** needs a guarded paid scrap test.
think: A smaller **night roster** could cut my higher wage even while the divider runs.
Ten months saved and **Leon’s pay** give time, not a replacement for lost premium.
do: **Compare** proposed night hours with four paid wage slips and a full camera trial.
**Learn** new AI weight display only on offered paid guarded trays checked by the lead.
**Apply** after actual cuts to posted safe local food jobs if base pay after travel covers bills.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic loss of night-rate income, despite a strong cushion.
S1.quote: A nice schedule cannot pay a shortfall.
fieldNote: Her **new AI learning** is active weight-display practice on guarded test biscuits, beyond occasional notice searches.
She makes **job moves** only after actual hour cuts and real safe postings whose net wage covers household costs.

steps.text: Compare posted night roster with four pay slips and day-shift camera evidence
Learn AI weight display only on offered paid guarded test trays with lead
Apply after night cuts to posted safe nearby food work if base pay after travel fits

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Leon that AGI could plan biscuit orders in 2028, while capable robots that feed and clean the divider arrive around 2031. I would ask the factory for dates and paid night jobs before it orders a new line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 63 when robots can do the physical biscuit work. I expect many divider shifts, including mine, to disappear; the night premium would be hard to match in another role. Ten months saved would buy a search, but I would lie awake wondering what pays the rent in month eleven.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would delay replacing the car while this one still runs and keep that cash for bills. I would take a recognised food-quality course only if a funded paid place includes supervised guarded practice at the stopped divider. If my hours fall after I pass, I would apply for posted safe local quality jobs only where base pay after travel and shift times meet our costs; if no course place is offered, I would apply to posted safe nearby packing work on the same terms while keeping any paid nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed by the likely loss of my main wage, even with savings. A course is useful only when a job and a real pay line follow it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would safe quality practice involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would weigh a light biscuit, reject a bad tray and stop the divider before clearing a roller. The trainer must watch me on a guarded stopped line; a login from home would not teach that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement make the job search unnecessary?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if written retirement income, Leon's pay and our other costs add up after rent and food. We have not done that arithmetic, so I would keep looking at paid jobs rather than assume a birthday settles it.

say: I would separate **2028 order AGI** from physical divider robots around 2031.
The plant should publish **paid night jobs** before changing the line.
think: At **63**, I expect many biscuit shifts, including mine, to vanish.
Ten months of **savings** may not replace a high night premium after that.
do: **Delay** the car replacement and keep cash for bills.
**Take** recognised food-quality training only with funded paid guarded stopped-line practice.
**Apply** after cuts to posted safe quality if qualified, or packing without a course, at usable pay.
feel: **Alarmed** by expected major wage loss and sleepless rent calculations.
S2.quote: Ten months saved would buy a search, but I would lie awake wondering what pays the rent in month eleven.
fieldNote: Her **2031 risk** is physical robot handling on the biscuit line, after 2028 AGI first changes planning.
The **quality and packing** routes require real safe postings with net after-travel wages, and retirement remains unproven.

steps.text: Delay planned car replacement and retain cash for bills
Take recognised food-quality course if funded paid guarded stopped-line place offered
Apply for posted safe local quality if qualified and cut, pay after travel and shifts fit
Apply for posted safe nearby packing if no course, pay after travel and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew AGI may plan biscuit runs in 2031, while capable robots that handle dough and cleanup arrive around 2034. Five years lets us look at actual paid course seats and the vacancies that follow them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 66 when those robots reach the physical line. I may be ready to stop by then, but that depends on actual income after rent and medical costs, not just a hope. If I still need wages, my junior standing means I cannot assume a protected night post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would add some newly earned premium pay to our reserve each full month after bills. I would enrol in a locally accepted bakery-quality certificate only if fees and release hours are paid and a trainer offers guarded stopped-line practice. After qualifying, if night hours fall, I would apply only for posted safe local quality roles whose base pay after travel and shifts cover our costs; if no real course place appears, I would look for posted food-packing work on those same terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage while our retirement figures remain open. Five years lets me see whether a course leads somewhere before I give up the night rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you check that the certificate is accepted?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask two nearby food plants which certificate their posted quality jobs require. If the college course is not on either list, I would keep working and ask about another offered place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the practical exam include?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would weigh a tray, record why a biscuit fails and isolate the divider before touching a sticky roller. A qualified trainer should watch each step, not sign a sheet after a video.

say: I would ask for **accepted paid courses** before 2034 robots reach biscuit work.
A **posted quality wage** matters more than a certificate title.
think: At **66**, I may still need work if retirement income falls short.
My **junior status** makes a protected night post uncertain.
do: **Save** newly paid night-premium money after household bills.
**Enrol** only in locally accepted quality training with funded fees, paid release and guarded trainer practice.
**Apply** after qualification and cuts to posted safe quality, or packing without a course, at viable net pay.
feel: **Anxious** about later income, with time to test accepted training and posted work.
S3.quote: A qualified trainer should watch each step, not sign a sheet after a video.
fieldNote: Her **course gate** includes local employer acceptance, funded fees, paid release and a supervised stopped divider.
The **two job searches** depend on real safe local postings whose base pay after travel covers living costs.

steps.text: Save new paid night-premium wages after household bills
Enrol in accepted quality course only if funded paid guarded trainer place offered
Apply for posted safe local quality if qualified and cut, pay after travel and shifts fit
Search posted safe local packing if no course, pay after travel and shifts fit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI could plan biscuit orders in 2036, while capable robots might run the divider around 2039. Ten years gives us time to compare work, savings and retirement numbers, provided we use the real ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 71 when robots can handle the line, if I am still employed. Leon and I may be able to stop before then, but we have not calculated a safe income after rent and health costs. Our high current wage and ten-month cushion make the next few years sound while that decision stays open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the night shift while it pays and request written retirement-income figures and a household cost list this year. I would take a locally accepted bakery-quality course only if fees and release are paid and a guarded supervised place fits my shift. If I am still working after 2036 and night hours fall, I would apply only to posted safe local food jobs whose regular wage after travel and shifts cover our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the far end, not worried about this month's rent. I would prefer an answer from actual figures over either a cheerful guess or a frightening headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would help with the retirement calculation?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Leon and I would compare the written estimate with rent, food, transport and medical costs; our grown daughter could help read the forms. I would not put our daughter's wages into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a job worth taking after 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A posting would need safe work, an actual base rate after travel and a shift I can manage. A vague promise of a night bonus would not replace the wage we have now.

say: I would keep **2036 planning AGI** separate from physical divider robots around 2039.
A decade permits **real income checks** before retirement or job changes.
think: At **71**, I may already have stopped if written income covers costs.
Our **current high pay** and ten-month reserve make near-term living secure.
do: **Keep** paid night shifts and request written retirement-income and cost figures.
**Take** accepted quality training only with funded fees, paid release and guarded supervision.
**Apply** after 2036 cuts if still employed to posted safe local food work at viable net wages.
feel: **Uneasy** about a distant decision while near-term pay remains sound.
S4.quote: A vague promise of a night bonus would not replace the wage we have now.
fieldNote: Her **retirement enquiry** does not commit to stopping; written income must cover rent and health costs first.
Any later **course or job** depends on accepted paid safe training or posted work with workable pay after travel.

steps.text: Keep working paid night divider shifts while available
Request written retirement income and household cost figures this year
Take accepted quality course only if funded paid guarded supervised place fits shift
Apply post-2036 after cuts to posted safe local food work if net pay and shifts fit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because capable robots around 2031 could remove my night-rate biscuit shift before we know whether retirement income is enough. A funded safe quality place, written paid-shift dates and posted local jobs at a workable net wage would help. I would not resign before an actual offer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask who cleans the divider when dough sticks at two in the morning. A biscuit line does not become efficient when its first tray is too light to sell. Somebody has to be paid for that correction.

headlineQuote: A biscuit line does not become efficient when its first tray is too light to sell.
portrait: **Dana**, 58, is a junior night-shift biscuit-divider operator with secondary education who is still learning the machine.
She and her **hospital-worker partner** Leon have grown children, a high night-rate wage and ten months of expenses saved.
She uses **AI occasionally** for notices after colleagues test it, and learns new controls only from paid guarded evidence.
Fast **2031 robots** alarm her about losing the premium; retirement remains conditional on written income after living and health costs.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could bring capable divider robots around 2031 and remove her higher paid night shifts.
whatWouldHelp: She wants **funded safe training**, written job dates, posted local net-wage offers and actual retirement-income figures.
